title.narrative: Ensuring safe public spaces and adequate housing in Beirut City

description.narrative:
On 4 August 2020, a large amount of ammonium nitrate stored at the Port of Beirut exploded, destroying much of the port and severely damaging dense residential and commercial areas within 5km of the site of the explosion. Areas located within 20km from the epicenter of the explosion sustained light to moderate damages. The disaster left more than 200 people dead, thousands injured and many homeless.
According to the Beirut Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment (RDNA), physical damages amount to approximately USD 3.8–4.6 billion, with housing and culture sectors most severely affected. The explosion is estimated to have caused between USD 1.9–2.3 billion in damage to the housing sector, directly impacting approximately 300,000 residents, including 60,000 families who have had their homes damaged, and 1,000 residents displaced due to being evacuated following severe structural damages to their homes. The explosion also damaged private and public schools and academic institutions, as well as healthcare centers and major hospitals. Public infrastructure and municipal services also suffered significant damage. Beirut and Bourj Hammoud were the most affected municipalities. Beirut suffered greater damage in the range of USD 20–25 million; however, Bourj Hammoud houses a large number of vulnerable people in congested locations, which poses risks of increased vulnerability. Around 50 per cent of the damaged municipal infrastructure was and still is the urban mobility systems (such as roads, bridges and related assets), which are critical for people’s living conditions and livelihoods. Many local parks, playgrounds, public squares and other communal facilities/buildings were also affected.
The proposed project aims to facilitate the recovery of Beirut through the rehabilitation of residential buildings/damaged households and a strategic public space impacted by the Beirut Port explosion – via an urban recovery approach and building back better, greener and more sustainably. The project will rely on existing data and maps collected by UN-Habitat Lebanon through another on-going project funded by the Lebanon Financing Facility (managed by the World Bank) in the explosion affected areas. The data collected includes legal status, occupancy of buildings, heritage value, and level of damage. Also, in close coordination with local and governmental authorities, the selection of the most vulnerable/marginalized populations (such as refugee/displaced and local children, youth, men, women, older persons, and PWD) will be validated. This data is coupled with a recently conducted survey by the Lebanese Armed Forces that shows the residential units that are still not rehabilitated after the explosion. This intervention will complement existing projects implemented by diverse stakeholders, including UN-Habitat – to maximize the impact on the geographical location, which has vast importance for the economic recovery of the country as a whole. It will target vulnerable populations, specifically female-headed households, refugees and vulnerable Lebanese. The project team will rely on existing data to identify the vulnerable beneficiaries, coupled with consultations, one-on-one meetings, and phone calls. Men and women from the affected communities will be engaged in rehabilitation and construction activities, thus contributing to restore their livelihoods. The project activities will focus on areas affected by the explosion, such as Gemmayzeh, Mar Mikhael and Karantina. In addition, the Project will target the Mar Mikhael Train Station which falls under the Directorate General of Railways and Public Transport. The station has a very strategic location and includes a number of small buildings that could be used for recreational, educational, and cultural heritage activities.
The project will be implemented in close coordination with concerned government institutions, specifically with the Municipality of Beirut (MoB)/Governor of Beirut (GoB) Office, Directorate General of Antiquities (DGA) and Directorate General of Railways and Public Transport. At the Municipality of Bourj Hammoud and MoB's request, UN-Habitat has deployed staff at both municipalities in the immediate aftermath of the explosion – and immediately supported in assessing the buildings' level of damage and providing expertise on digitizing the impact assessment using mobile technology, Geographic Information System (GIS) and mapping services. This ongoing close coordination with the concerned authorities has placed UN-Habitat at the heart of the coordination of the shelter/building back better response, thus enabling targeted interventions through the support of partners. The proposed project would meet medium-term needs already expressed by the MoB. UN-Habitat has existing projects in Beirut, relevant technical and operational expertise and many years of excellent cooperation which would ensure the success and permissions to implement the proposed project.
